territorial_scope.description: Applies to exports and transfers from the United States to the PRC and reaches foreign persons who transact covered technology with the PRC.

evidence.quote: a foreign person that, on or after the date of the enactment of this Act, knowingly sells or otherwise provides to, or knowingly purchases from, the People's Republic of China

summary.short: Directs the President to control exports and transfers to China of covered national interest technology or intellectual property, starting 180 days after enactment. Authorises IEEPA blocking of foreign persons who knowingly sell, provide or buy such technology with China, and requires a USTR list of Chinese products.
summary.long: Directs the President to control exports, re-exports and transfers to the People's Republic of China of covered national interest technology or intellectual property, starting 180 days after enactment, with regulations due within 180 days and a joint State-Commerce report due within 90 days assessing whether ITAR or EAR controls should apply. Covered technology includes items contributing to PRC military potential detrimental to US national security, components of listed products, and technology used for human rights violations; 'technology' expressly includes artificial intelligence, computing and robotics. Section 5 directs blocking of property under IEEPA of foreign persons who knowingly sell, provide or purchase such technology with the PRC, and of Chinese persons who knowingly use it in violation of section 4 or other US export controls, subject to a national security waiver and an exclusion for importation of goods. Section 6 adds Trade Act section 183, requiring the USTR to list, within 120 days and annually, PRC products receiving Made in China 2025 support or used for human rights violations, including products in artificial intelligence, high-capacity computing, semiconductors, quantum computing and robotics. Section 3 is a sense-of-Congress statement.

notes: Introduced bill text; no consolidated version. Cited instruments are US Code titles and statutes without registry IDs, so target_instrument_id is left empty and identified in target_text. Internal inconsistency: Sec. 2(4) defines 'knowingly' as actual knowledge 'or should have known', which the text does not reconcile with the actual-knowledge standard in the same definition. Sec. 4(a) sets the control obligation at 180 days after enactment, while Sec. 4(b) requires the report at 90 days. Sec. 5 applies to 'covered national interest technology' defined in Sec. 2(2) by reference to a list under the new Trade Act section 183 (Sec. 6).

thresholds.note: No numeric cutoff in the text changes legal treatment of a person, entity, product or service. The numeric periods in Sec. 4(a), 4(b), 4(c), Sec. 6 (new Trade Act Sec. 183(a)) and the 180-day start of the export control are procedural deadlines or phase-in dates recorded as events, not thresholds. The penalty provisions in Sec. 5(e)(2) cross-reference IEEPA Sections 206(b) and (c) without stating amounts, so they are enforcement rather than thresholds. Sec. 2(5)(C) cites a 1946 Act date, which is not a cutoff. The product lists in Sec. 183(b) are classifications, not numeric thresholds.
